appraisal_events.evidence: Charlus "quitta brusquement M. de Faffenheim avec qui il causait" to intercept him and, in the doorway, "Puisque je vois que vous allez dans le monde maintenant, faites-moi donc le plaisir de venir me voir... Voulez-vous faire deux pas avec moi ?" — said "d'un air d'inattention et de calcul", as of a pleasure he feared losing if the chance escaped him.
appraisal_events.explanation: The baron abandons a prince mid-conversation to solicit the narrator's visits and company, an overture that raises the young man while the narration exposes the studied carelessness and eagerness behind it.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Il est en train de parler avec cet idiot de duc de Guermantes" — "C'est charmant ce que vous dites là, je le dirai à mon frère"; then "— Qui est-ce qui vous parle de M. de Charlus ? me dit le baron d'un air insolent. Allez auprès de Robert." The narrator also warns him he has taken another visitor's hat and is answered "Vous voulez m'empêcher de prendre mon chapeau ?"
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's two sallies both misfire — he insults the baron's brother to his face and shows he does not know who Charlus is or that the ducal hat is rightfully his — and Charlus answers with insolence and a command that dismisses him.

appraisal_events.evidence: "vous avez participé ce matin à un de ces déjeuners d'orgie qu'il a avec une femme qui le déshonore. Vous devriez bien user de votre influence sur lui pour lui faire comprendre le chagrin qu'il cause à sa pauvre mère et à nous tous en traînant notre nom dans la boue".
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus arraigns Saint-Loup in the family's name for a liaison that dishonours him, though the inflated language of orgies, delivered by a man who has just been arbitrarily insolent over a stolen hat, keeps the indignation at a slight distance.

status_effects.explanation: Charlus opens his door to him — asks him to write, to call, to walk out with him — admitting him to a private access he had not had.

Both of his remarks collapse under him — the insult to the duke lands on the duke's brother, and his question about M. de Charlus betrays that he does not know whom he is addressing — and he is answered with insolence and sent away.
He turns each of the narrator's blunders back on him and closes the exchange with an order, holding the upper hand in the doorway.
In his uncle's mouth he is a man dishonoured by his mistress, grieving his mother and dragging the family name through the mud.

ambiguities: The narrator does not know that Charlus is a Guermantes and the duke's brother, so he reads the ducal-coronet hat as a stolen one and takes "M. de Charlus" for a third person; the snub lands on his ignorance rather than on any fault of manner.
